clue.text: Crown has literally the first and last jewel

parts.note: the crown of something is its top
taken literally, the first and last letters of the alphabet are A and Z

explanation.surface: A royal crown boasts the finest of all gems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' tells you to take 'the first and last' as letters: A and Z open and close the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellow gemstone is a classic precious stone set in jewellery.

clue.text: Young Cratchit also elated here in Africa ?

definitions.text: Young Cratchit also elated here in Africa ?

parts.words: Young Cratchit also elated here in Africa ?
parts.note: the youngest Cratchit in Dickens's A Christmas Carol is Tiny Tim; 'Tim bucked too' (Tim also elated) said quickly sounds like the old spelling of a remote city in Mali

explanation.walkthrough: BUCKED is a British colloquialism for cheered up or elated. The question mark signals that the place name is reached by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabled remote city in Mali on the edge of the Sahara, now usually spelt Timbuktu.

clue.text: George is director automatically

parts.note: George was RAF slang for the automatic flying system of an aircraft, so George steers a plane automatically

explanation.walkthrough: 'George' is not a person but airmen's slang for the autopilot.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who steers an aircraft or ship, here the automatic device that does the steering.

clue.text: Persian Seer put up a little weight on a very hot day

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means written upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: OZ is the abbreviation for ounce, a small weight
a roaster is a colloquial name for a scorching day

explanation.surface: A Persian prophet gains a few ounces during a heatwave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' in a down clue reverses OZ to ZO, which goes on top of ROASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Persian prophet who founded the Zoroastrian religion is a famous seer.

clue.text: Will he barge in rudely in an hour with news of what's coming?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters sit within the abbreviation for an hour, so this word signals the insertion

parts.note: HR is the standard abbreviation for hour

indicators.note: barging in rudely suggests a rough disorder, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a rude visitor will burst in within the hour bearing news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rudely' rearranges BARGE IN to ARBINGE, and 'in' puts that inside HR, the abbreviation for an hour. 'Will he' only sets the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A forerunner or sign that announces something approaching is exactly a herald of future events.

clue.text: A measure for teacher reorganization

indicators.note: reorganization means the letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A new policy is introduced to restructure the teaching staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reorganization' rearranges TEACHER.
explanation.definitionFit: A metric unit of land area equal to ten thousand square metres.

clue.text: Egyptian Place of Stone

parts.note: the inscribed stone that unlocked hieroglyphs was found at an Egyptian town and named after it

explanation.walkthrough: The Rosetta Stone, now in the British Museum, takes its name from the town in the Nile Delta where it was found in 1799.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in the Nile Delta, where the famous trilingual inscribed stone was discovered.

clue.text: Suffer terrible ruin when about 100

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the Roman numeral, so this word signals the container
terrible ruin is ruin in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone suffers financial disaster when they owe about a hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges RUIN to INUR, and 'about' wraps it round C.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something unwelcome upon yourself, such as a debt or penalty, is to sustain it.

clue.text: Well-bred, they show the quality of the opposite sex

definitions.text: Well-bred, they show the quality of the opposite sex

parts.words: Well-bred, they show the quality of the opposite sex
parts.note: split in two, the word is gentle plus men: males showing gentleness, a quality traditionally credited to women

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it describes men who are gentle, the 'quality of the opposite sex' in an old-fashioned view.
explanation.definitionFit: Courteous, well-mannered men of good breeding.

clue.text: Revive point taken by Descartes

parts.note: René Descartes, the French philosopher
W, west, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A philosopher's argument is brought back to life when Descartes adopts it.
explanation.walkthrough: W, a compass point, is taken by (added to) RENE, the philosopher's first name. 'Point' looks like an argument, but it is a compass direction.
explanation.definitionFit: To restore or make new again is to bring back to life or freshness.

clue.text: Waters for Lancashire lasses to run in?

definitions.text: Waters for Lancashire lasses to run in?

parts.words: Waters for Lancashire lasses to run in?
parts.note: Lancashire was cotton-mill country, so its working girls were mill girls; a race they might run would be a mill race, the channel of water driving a mill wheel

explanation.walkthrough: Lancashire, a county in north-west England, was the heart of the cotton-mill industry, so its lasses suggest mill workers.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the fast channels of water that carry the current to turn a water wheel.

clue.text: Type in a chapter

definitions.meaning: a large size of printing type, once a standard printer's name
a clergyman who belongs to the chapter of a cathedral

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a printer's type size of about 48 points, and a cathedral clergyman who sits in its chapter.

clue.text: Cult centre art backed by extremist

indicators.note: only the central letters of the word cult are kept here
art backed means the word art is written backwards

explanation.surface: An extremist sect's headquarters puts its money behind art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre' takes UL from the middle of CULT; 'backed' turns ART into TRA.
explanation.definitionFit: A person holding extreme views, especially in politics, was called this, from Latin for beyond.

clue.text: Bright evidence of Apollo's departure

parts.note: Apollo was the Greek god of the sun, so his departure is sunset, and the bright evidence left behind is the glow in the sky after it

explanation.walkthrough: Apollo here is not the space mission but the sun god, whose leaving is sunset.
explanation.definitionFit: The light lingering in the western sky after sunset is a glow that comes after the sun has gone.

clue.text: Part support for the board

parts.note: a table top or board is held up by a pair of A-shaped stands, each one part of the support

explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' suggests a company's directors, but it is a plank or table top resting on stands.
explanation.definitionFit: A framework of a beam on splayed legs, used in pairs to hold up a table top.

clue.text: Company so well run shows measure of expansion

indicators.note: the company's letters together with the answer show the longer word, so taking them away leaves the answer

parts.note: a coefficient of expansion measures how much a material grows when heated

explanation.surface: A well-managed firm shows signs of growth.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says CO plus the answer gives COEFFICIENT, as in coefficient of expansion; remove CO to find the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Working smoothly without waste is the mark of something competently organised.

clue.text: Lamb, say, strange and unfathomable

indicators.note: something strange is odd or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finds Charles Lamb, for example, an odd and impenetrable writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb, say' looks like an example of something (the essayist, or meat), but the two words are just letters: 'strange' rearranges LAMBSAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so deep that it cannot be sounded, like the ocean depths, is bottomless.

clue.text: It calls for a pull-up in a shanty

definitions.text: It calls for a pull-up in a shanty

parts.words: It calls for a pull-up in a shanty
parts.note: a sea shanty's chorus cry sung by sailors as they haul together on a rope

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shanty' looks like a hut, but it is a sailors' work song; 'pull-up' is hauling on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional sailors' chant used to keep time when heaving on a rope or capstan.

clue.text: Back-breaking end of the gleaning

parts.note: gleaners pick up the final stalks from a harvested field; the proverbial camel's back breaks under one final stalk

explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'the straw that broke the camel's back': a small final burden that makes things unbearable.
explanation.definitionFit: The final small trouble that makes a situation intolerable, from the proverbial straw that broke the camel's back.

clue.text: Made proposal. It's not on -a broken reed

parts.note: a switch that is not on is off

indicators.note: a broken reed is in pieces, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone made a suggestion and was told it was unacceptable, relying on a weak person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges REED to ERED, placed after OFF. 'A broken reed' is an idiom for an unreliable person, which is the surface's misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward or tender something for acceptance is the past tense of proffer.

clue.text: Line produced by a ruler

parts.note: a ruler suggests a measuring stick drawing a line, but here it is a monarch producing a line of descendants

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' looks like the straight-edge, but it is a sovereign whose heirs form a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A succession of rulers from the same family, such as the Tudors.

clue.text: Rears in order-to be farm workers

parts.note: a hind is an old word for a farm labourer, especially in Scotland and northern England

explanation.surface: Someone raises children so they can grow up to work the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rears' looks like a verb (brings up), but it is the plural noun for bottoms. HIND is an old British word for a farmhand.
explanation.definitionFit: Backsides or bottoms are colloquially called this, the hind parts of the body.

clue.text: Island security post in a way

definitions.text: Island security post in a way

parts.words: Island security post in a way
parts.note: a short sturdy post on a traffic island in a road, guarding it from vehicles

explanation.walkthrough: A traffic island is a raised refuge in the middle of a road; 'a way' is a road. The posts also secure ships' ropes on a quay.
explanation.definitionFit: A short thick post, used on traffic islands or quaysides for mooring ships.

clue.text: It ran cold perhaps, like what teacher said

indicators.note: perhaps signals that these letters might be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A tap or stream ran cold, perhaps, just as the teacher had said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges ITRANCOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to teaching or a body of taught principles, from Latin doctrina, instruction.

clue.text: Hidden encouragement by a greyhound fan

definitions.meaning: to lie low and keep quiet
split as two words it is the cry '...!' from a racegoer at a greyhound track

explanation.definitionFit: Lying low in concealment is British slang 'lying doggo'; and a racing fan would shout 'dog, go!' at a running hound.

clue.text: Later sort of honey-badger

indicators.note: sort here works as a verb meaning arrange, so the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Later, a sort of honey badger appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges LATER.
explanation.definitionFit: An African and Asian burrowing mammal of the weasel family, fond of honey.

clue.text: Painter in classic art portrays French scene

indicators.note: the painter's letters are placed within the Latin word for art

parts.note: ars is the Latin, or classical, word for art
RA stands for Royal Academician, a painter elected to the Royal Academy

explanation.surface: An artist working in the classical tradition depicts a view of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' means Latin here, giving ARS. ARRAS is a town in northern France, scene of First World War battles, and also gave its name to tapestry.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in northern France, the scene of heavy fighting in the First World War.

clue.text: Figure for a diamond

parts.note: the geometrical figure shaped like the diamond on playing cards, an equal-sided parallelogram

explanation.walkthrough: 'Diamond' suggests a gem, but it is the shape, as on a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhombus, an equilateral parallelogram, is the shape known as a diamond.

clue.text: Conjectural visitor ?

parts.note: a caller to a house whose name, said out loud, matches a word meaning supposed or surmised

explanation.walkthrough: The word for a visitor sounds like 'guessed', which is what conjectural means; the question mark marks the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone invited to stay at a home or attend an event as a visitor.

clue.text: Jaques' entrance to 'the world ?

parts.note: in As You Like It, Jaques says all the world's a stage, so the entrance to that world would be the actors' way into a theatre

explanation.walkthrough: Jaques is the melancholy lord in Shakespeare's As You Like It, who begins 'All the world's a stage'.
explanation.definitionFit: The back entrance of a theatre used by performers and staff, leading to the area behind the scenes.

clue.text: Retreat sounded for batsman so defeated ?

definitions.text: Retreat sounded for batsman so defeated ?

parts.words: Retreat sounded for batsman so defeated ?
parts.note: a batsman given out has the retreat to the pavilion played for him, as a bugle plays a retreat, and he has been beaten

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a dismissed batsman is OUT; a retreat is PLAYED on a bugle. Together they make a word for beaten at a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten by superior skill in a game or contest.

clue.text: Neat bend in the river

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so a single one is an ox
a bow is a curve or bend, like a bent bow

explanation.surface: A tidy curve in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like 'tidy', but it is the old word for cattle, giving OX. The whole clue also describes the U-shaped loop a river makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A horseshoe-shaped loop in a meandering river, shaped like the collar of a yoke.
